analysis.one_liner: Makes employers investigate harassment and discrimination complaints and voids settlement agreements that silence workers from reporting misconduct to authorities.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2022 and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or any action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers to set up a confidential process for reporting harassment, discrimination, and retaliation, investigate complaints promptly and neutrally, and give workers written notice of the outcome. It also would have made settlement agreements unenforceable when their nondisclosure clauses stop workers from telling Congress, government agencies, or law enforcement about unlawful conduct, required a plain-language notice of that right in every settlement, and given workers at least 21 days to consider an agreement. It never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who experience discrimination, harassment, or retaliation at work, and whistleblowers who might otherwise be silenced by settlement agreements. Under the bill, any employee could report misconduct confidentially, would get a neutral investigation with notice of the outcome, and could not be blocked by an NDA from telling Congress, regulators, or law enforcement about unlawful conduct. Workers would also get 21 days to consider a settlement and 7 days to change their mind after signing.

how_it_helps.text: It requires every employer to set up a confidential process for reporting discrimination, harassment, and retaliation, with prompt, neutral investigation and notice to the employee of the outcome.

It makes nondisclosure clauses in settlement agreements unenforceable when they block workers from telling Congress, government agencies, or law enforcement about unlawful discrimination, harassment, or retaliation.

It requires a plain-language notice in every settlement agreement stating that nothing prevents the worker from reporting misconduct to authorities, plus a 21-day window to consider the agreement and 7 days to rescind it.
It lets the EEOC enforce these rules, treating violations like Title VII discrimination claims.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would bear the cost of building complaint processes, conducting neutral investigations, and documenting compliance, and who would lose the ability to enforce nondisclosure clauses that keep misconduct claims out of public view. Taxpayers would fund new EEOC rulemaking and enforcement.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively, making unenforceable nondisclosure clauses in settlement agreements already signed before enactment (Section 6), which employers and some businesses would argue reopens settled deals and creates legal uncertainty.

It imposes new one-size-fits-all process requirements on every employer—mandatory investigation procedures, written reports to the accuser, 21-day consideration windows—which small businesses would bear as real compliance and legal costs.

Mandating notification of investigation outcomes and detailed documentation of the procedure could compromise confidentiality interests of all parties, including accused employees who are later cleared.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—workers able to report discrimination, harassment, and retaliation without being legally silenced and able to expect a real investigation—is significant and largely uncontroversial; Congress had already barred pre-dispute arbitration NDAs for sexual harassment claims in 2022 on a bipartisan basis. The costs are real but modest: employers face compliance and paperwork burdens, and the retroactive application to agreements already signed raises fairness and legal-transition objections an honest supporter would have to acknowledge. The bill's weakest point was design: it was introduced late in the session with no Republican cosponsor and never advanced, so it was never tested or improved in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and sat there until the two-year Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a vote, or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on June 17, 2022, late in the second session of the 117th Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day; no markup, hearing, or committee vote followed.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who use nondisclosure clauses in settlement agreements keep that tool; no one had to comply with new reporting and investigation requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using NDAs to settle claims

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, though the bill never advanced far enough for a floor test of bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Employers (especially large employers and those facing harassment/discrimination suits)
industries.note: The bill would require workplace reporting and investigation processes, limit the enforceability of nondisclosure clauses in settlement agreements, and apply those limits retroactively—reducing employers' ability to quietly settle misconduct claims with gag clauses. Compliance costs fall on employers; workers gain the leverage.

industries.industry: Employment lawyers and complainants in workplace disputes
industries.note: By making NDAs covering disclosure to government entities unenforceable, the bill would strengthen workers' ability to pursue legal redress and speak to authorities, and could increase demand for legal representation in workplace misconduct cases.
